title: Colors, Backgrounds and Borders
subtitle: Give Your Interfaces a Professional Visual Language
description: Learn how to control colors, backgrounds and borders, then use them together to transform a plain interface into a polished application dashboard.

blocks.text: Welcome to Lesson 3
Open your code editor.
Today, we are going to make our interface look like a real application.
You already know that HTML gives an application its structure.
You also learned that selectors allow CSS to target specific elements.
Now we are going to control the visual language of those elements.
That means choosing colors, backgrounds and borders.
Do not think of these as decorations.
These properties help users understand what is important on a real website or app.
By the end of the CSS course, you should be able to use these ideas to build complete interfaces.
So every example today will move us closer to that goal.

blocks.text: Run this page before adding CSS.
Look carefully at how plain it appears.
That is exactly what we want.
We are going to transform it step by step.
1. Changing Text Color
Let's begin with the simplest visual change.
CSS uses the color property to change the color of text.
Watch what happens when we target the main heading.

blocks.title: Changing Text Color
blocks.output: The Code Academy heading becomes cyan.

blocks.text: Run the page again.
Notice that only the heading changed.
That happened because our selector targeted only that heading.
This is where selectors and properties begin working together.
The selector answers where the style should go.
The property answers what should change.
Now you try changing the paragraph color.

blocks.title: Styling Supporting Text
blocks.output: The supporting text becomes a softer gray-blue.

blocks.text: Think about why we did not use the same color for everything.
Different colors can create visual hierarchy.
Important information can stand out while supporting information stays quieter.
2. Understanding Color Values
CSS gives you several ways to describe colors.
You can use color names.
You can use hexadecimal values.
You can also use RGB and RGBA values.

blocks.title: Different Color Formats
blocks.output: Each rule describes a blue color using a different CSS color format.

blocks.text: In professional interfaces, hexadecimal colors are very common.
They also make it easy to create a consistent color system.
For our dashboard, we will use a small group of colors instead of random colors everywhere.
This is an important habit when building real products.
3. Creating the Main Background
A website does not have to use a white background.
Let's create a dark application-style background.

blocks.title: Application Background
blocks.output: The entire page receives a dark background and light default text.

blocks.text: Run the page.
Look at how dramatically the interface changed with only two properties.
This is why understanding CSS fundamentals is so powerful.
A few carefully chosen rules can completely change the experience.
Now we need to separate the header from the rest of the page.
4. Styling a Header Background
Let's give the header its own background.

blocks.title: Header Background
blocks.output: The header becomes a separate dark panel.

blocks.text: Notice that we have introduced padding even though today's main topic is color.
That is intentional.
Real interfaces rarely use one CSS concept at a time.
You will constantly combine properties to create complete components.
That is the skill we are building throughout this course.
Now let's make the cards feel like separate application components.
5. Card Backgrounds

blocks.title: Creating Application Cards
blocks.output: Each course becomes a dark card against the page background.

blocks.text: Run your page.
Can you see the difference between the page and the cards?
We have created a visual layer.
This same idea is used in dashboards, banking apps, learning platforms and social applications.
A card is not just a box.
It is a way of grouping related information so the user can understand the interface.
Next, we will make those cards easier to distinguish.
6. Borders
A border draws a visual boundary around an element.
The basic border syntax is simple.

blocks.title: Adding a Border
blocks.output: A subtle border appears around every card.

blocks.text: Look closely at the border.
It is visible, but it does not overpower the content.
That is usually better than using an extremely strong border everywhere.
A professional interface often uses subtle visual separation.
Now let's make the corners smoother.
7. Rounded Corners

blocks.title: Rounding the Cards
blocks.output: The sharp card corners become rounded.

blocks.text: Run the page again.
Compare the rounded cards with the original sharp boxes.
Border radius is commonly used in modern application interfaces.
You will see it again when we build buttons, forms, navigation panels and other components.
Remember this pattern.
Background creates the surface.
Border defines the boundary.
Border radius changes the shape of the boundary.
8. Styling Buttons
Now we reach one of the most important elements in an application.
The button tells the user that an action is available.

blocks.title: Creating a Primary Button
blocks.output: The Continue buttons become bright primary action buttons.

blocks.text: Run the page.
Look at where your eyes go first.
The bright button attracts attention.
This is visual hierarchy in action.
Later, JavaScript can make this button perform an action.
For example, it could open a lesson, save information or move the user to another screen.
CSS controls how the action looks.
JavaScript will later control what the action does.
9. Creating a Consistent Color System
A real application should not have a different color for every element.
Instead, choose a small set of colors and reuse them.

blocks.title: Our Dashboard Color System
blocks.output: The dashboard now has a reusable set of design colors.

blocks.text: These are CSS custom properties.
They allow us to reuse the same design values throughout an application.
This becomes extremely useful when an application grows.
Imagine having hundreds of buttons and cards.
You want them to follow the same visual system.

blocks.title: Using the Color System
blocks.output: The components now use the shared color system.

blocks.text: 10. Background Images
Backgrounds can contain more than a solid color.
CSS can also place an image behind content.

blocks.title: Background Image
blocks.output: The hero section uses an image as its background.

blocks.text: The cover value tells the image to cover the available area.
Center controls where the image is positioned.
No-repeat prevents the image from being tiled.
You will use these properties in landing pages, profile screens and application headers.
11. Making the Dashboard Feel Like a Real Product
Now we are going to combine what you have learned.
Do not copy this blindly.
Look at each rule and ask what visual problem it solves.

blocks.title: Dashboard Visual System
blocks.output: A polished dark learning dashboard with a clear visual hierarchy.

blocks.text: Run the complete dashboard.
Now compare it with the plain version from the beginning.
You have not changed the HTML structure.
You changed the visual system with CSS.
That is one of the most important ideas in frontend development.

Pause here.
Before running the next example, predict what will happen.

blocks.question: You want to change only the text color of an element. Which property should you use?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The color property controls the text color.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Think about which property directly controls the color of text.
blocks.reasoning: The color property changes an element's text color, while background-color affects the area behind the content.
blocks.suggestion: Look at the difference between the text itself and the surface behind it.

blocks.question: A dashboard card needs a dark surface while the page behind it remains slightly darker. Which property is most appropriate for the card?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. background-color controls the card's surface.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about whether you are changing text, a border, or the surface behind the content.
blocks.reasoning: background-color paints the background area of the selected element.
blocks.suggestion: Ask yourself: which property controls what is behind the card's text?

blocks.question: Which rule creates a subtle one-pixel border around a card?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Both A and B are valid CSS border declarations.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Look closely at the syntax. CSS allows the border width, style and color to be written in different orders.
blocks.reasoning: The shorthand border property accepts width, style and color, and their order does not have to be exactly the same.
blocks.suggestion: Check whether both declarations contain a width, a border style and a color.

blocks.question: A developer wants the corners of a card to become rounded. Which property should be added?
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The property is related to borders, but think about which one changes the shape of the corners.
blocks.reasoning: border-radius rounds the corners of an element.
blocks.suggestion: Look for the property that describes the radius of a corner.

blocks.question: Your primary action button should stand out against a dark card. Which combination is most suitable?
options: Primary background with strong readable text
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A primary action should be visually distinguishable and readable.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about what should happen when a user needs to find the main action quickly.
blocks.reasoning: Primary actions usually need enough contrast and visual distinction to communicate their importance.
blocks.suggestion: Ask yourself which option would make the button easiest to identify.

blocks.question: Which CSS declaration makes an image cover the available background area?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. background-size: cover makes the image cover the available area.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Focus on the property that controls the size of a background image.
blocks.reasoning: background-size controls how the background image is sized. The cover value scales it to cover the available area.
blocks.suggestion: Look for the property that controls background image size.

blocks.text: 13. Final Application Challenge
Now imagine you are building a real learning application.
The dashboard needs a dark page background.
The course cards need slightly lighter surfaces.
Each card needs a subtle border.
The corners should be rounded.
The Continue button should use the primary color.
Your task is to build that visual system yourself.
Start with the page background.
Then style the cards.
Then style the buttons.
Run your page after every important change.
Do not worry if your first attempt is not perfect.
The goal is to learn how to control the interface.

blocks.title: Final Challenge Starting Point
blocks.output: A minimally styled dashboard ready for your visual design.

blocks.question: You want the page background to be #0A0F1E while each card uses #121A2B. Which approach correctly separates the two surfaces?
options: Use color instead of background-color for both
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The body and cards can have different background colors.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about which selector represents the whole page and which selector represents each card.
blocks.reasoning: The body controls the main page surface, while .card controls the card surface.
blocks.suggestion: Match each color to the element it is supposed to visually represent.

blocks.question: A card currently has a background but no visible boundary. Which change most directly adds that boundary?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A border creates the visual boundary around the card.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The question asks for a boundary around the element, not a text or background change.
blocks.reasoning: The border property draws a boundary around the selected element.
blocks.suggestion: Think about the difference between the inside surface and the line around it.

blocks.text: What You Can Build From This
You have just learned more than how to change colors.
You learned how visual decisions can communicate information.
You learned how backgrounds create surfaces.
You learned how borders separate components.
You learned how rounded corners shape components.
You learned how a color system keeps an application consistent.
These are the same building blocks you will use in larger interfaces.
Soon, these cards can become course dashboards.
Those dashboards can become complete application screens.
And those screens can eventually become complete websites and applications.
HTML gives us structure.
CSS gives that structure its visual language.
JavaScript will later give our interfaces behavior.
Keep that bigger goal in mind as we continue.
We are not learning CSS just to write CSS.
We are learning CSS so you can eventually build real things.
